body.claim: Trying to recall something from memory strengthens it more, in the long run, than looking at it again.
body.why: Studies of the testing effect find that restudied words are remembered better right after practice, but tested words are remembered better as time moves on. Researchers think tests work as learning opportunities, because pulling an answer out of memory takes effort.

probes.question: As time passes, which tends to be remembered better?
True or false: restudying tends to give higher recall right after practice than testing does.

claims.claim: Tested words are remembered better as time passes than restudied (title, claim, probe 1)
claims.quote: whereas tested words were higher as time moves on.

claims.claim: Restudied words are recalled better right after practice (why; probe 2 true)
claims.quote: Retrieval strength (also known as recall accuracy) is typically higher for restudied words when tested immediately after practice

claims.claim: Researchers think tests work as learning opportunities
claims.quote: some authors believe is due to limited retrieval success during practice supporting the idea that tests are learning opportunities
claims.note: Page says 'some authors believe'; card says 'researchers think', acceptable.

claims.claim: Pulling an answer out of memory takes effort (why)
claims.quote: difficult but successful retrievals are better for memory than easier successful retrievals
claims.note: Retrieval effort hypothesis on the page; card's 'because' is a fair paraphrase.
